summary: Several Bellevue admission numbers belong to more than one patient — 'a clerical economy'.
Cell 66 held a deformed man pulled from a cellar in Innsmouth.
The Cell 66 patient was found in a cellar under an old Marsh property.
Men with federal papers took the Cell 66 patient; the attendant signed the release unread, for money.
The Cell 66 patient left Bellevue through the laundry in a linen cart, onto a freight car for Boston.
The Bellevue freight car went to the Federal Quarantine Docks, Boston.
Robbie the orderly heard the Cell 66 patient singing through the wall, and sang back.
Robbie's iron lockbox held the Cell 66 patient's sealed effects (admission 32-066).
Zadok Allen panics at the word 'Innsmouth'.
A Bellevue patient is entered under an alias; the real surname is Marsh.
The Chief Attendant believes the sea is calling some patients home — and that the investigators will be admitted in time.
An investigator threatened the Chief Attendant in front of his staff.
The 'family release' shown at Bellevue was a forgery.
The investigators are not federal agents.
None of the investigators is Marsh kin.
